title: Arrays & Associative Arrays
summary: Bash arrays are underused and misunderstood. Indexed arrays for lists, associative arrays for key-value maps — both are essential for writing scripts that don't fall apart on filenames with spaces.

sections.title: Indexed arrays
sections.body:
## Indexed Arrays: Safe Lists in Bash

Bash is often used as if it only has strings and integers, but it has had proper array support since version 3. The reason arrays matter is subtle but important: when you store a list of items in a plain string variable, you face an irresolvable conflict. If items are separated by spaces, any item that contains a space breaks your iteration. If items are separated by newlines, you cannot use the variable in a simple `for` loop without word-splitting side effects. There is no separator character that is guaranteed to never appear in the values.

An indexed array sidesteps this entirely. Each element is stored separately, with no separator character at all — bash tracks the boundary between elements internally. A pod name with spaces, a path with spaces, a label value with special characters — all of these are stored and retrieved correctly. The `"${arr[@]}"` expansion (with double quotes) expands each element as a separate word, regardless of its content.

The other key advantage of arrays is that they let you use `readarray -t` (also called `mapfile -t`) to populate a list from command output **one line per element**, without any of the word-splitting and glob-expansion hazards that come with `arr=($(command))`. This is the single most important array technique for Kubernetes scripting, where you routinely need to iterate over lists of pod names, namespace names, or deployment names returned by `kubectl`.

In the DevOps context, arrays appear most commonly as: lists of namespaces to process, lists of deployments to check, lists of image names to scan, or lists of environments to deploy to. They are the right data structure whenever you have a sequence of values that you want to iterate over safely.

**Why:** without arrays you end up doing fragile things like `PODS=$(kubectl get pods | awk '{print $1}')` and iterating over a string. When a pod name has a space (or your output has a blank line), it breaks. Arrays fix this.

```bash
# Declare and populate
pods=("argocd-server-abc" "argocd-repo-server-xyz" "argocd-redis-123")

# Access by index
echo "${pods[0]}"           # argocd-server-abc
echo "${pods[-1]}"          # last element: argocd-redis-123

# All elements
echo "${pods[@]}"           # space-separated (use in loops)
echo "${pods[*]}"           # same but respects IFS

# Length
echo "${#pods[@]}"          # 3

# Slice: elements 1 and 2
echo "${pods[@]:1:2}"

# Append
pods+=("argocd-dex-456")

# Iterate safely (handles spaces in names)
for pod in "${pods[@]}"; do
    echo "Checking: $pod"
done

# Build array from command output — readarray is the safe way
# (don't do: pods=($( kubectl get pods )) — breaks on spaces)
readarray -t pods < <(kubectl get pods -n argocd --no-headers -o custom-columns=":metadata.name")

for pod in "${pods[@]}"; do
    restarts=$(kubectl get pod "$pod" -n argocd -o jsonpath='{.status.containerStatuses[0].restartCount}')
    echo "$pod: $restarts restarts"
done

# Delete element
unset 'pods[1]'

# Delete whole array
unset pods
```

sections.title: Associative arrays (dictionaries)
sections.body:
## Associative Arrays: Key-Value Maps in Bash

Indexed arrays store ordered sequences. Associative arrays (also called dictionaries or hash maps) store **key-value pairs**, where each value is accessed by a meaningful name rather than a position. This distinction matters in practice: when you are mapping environment names to kubeconfig contexts, namespace names to ArgoCD app names, or cluster names to their API endpoints, an associative array expresses the relationship directly and makes the code self-documenting.

The alternative — using parallel indexed arrays or repeated `grep` and `sed` to look up values from a flat text format — is fragile and hard to maintain. Parallel arrays (`envs=(prod staging)` + `contexts=(eks-prod eks-staging)`) fall out of sync when someone edits one without updating the other. Repeated grep against a flat file is slow and error-prone. An associative array keeps the mapping in one place, makes lookups fast and readable (`${context_map[$env]}`), and fails safely when a key is missing (you can test with `[[ -v map[key] ]]` before accessing).

The one important constraint: associative arrays must be explicitly declared with `declare -A` before use. Unlike indexed arrays (which bash infers from the `arr=(...)` syntax), bash needs to know you want associative semantics before you start assigning keys. Forgetting `declare -A` is the most common mistake with associative arrays, and bash's error message in that case is not always obvious.

In Kubernetes environments, associative arrays are particularly useful for configuration that varies by environment: different namespaces, different contexts, different replicas counts, different alert thresholds — all of which change based on where you are deploying. Centralizing this configuration in an associative array at the top of the script makes it easy to review and update without touching the logic.

**Why:** when you need to map one thing to another — namespace to cost, pod to status, env to kubecontext — associative arrays beat parallel arrays or repeated grep.

```bash
# Must declare explicitly
declare -A context_map

context_map["prod"]="eks-prod-mach-x7kq"
context_map["staging"]="eks-staging"
context_map["dev"]="minikube"

# Access
echo "${context_map[prod]}"

# Check if key exists
if [[ -v context_map[prod] ]]; then
    echo "prod context: ${context_map[prod]}"
fi

# All keys
echo "${!context_map[@]}"

# All values
echo "${context_map[@]}"

# Iterate
for env in "${!context_map[@]}"; do
    echo "$env -> ${context_map[$env]}"
done

# Practical: map namespaces to their ArgoCD app names
declare -A ns_to_app=(
    ["argocd"]="argocd-app"
    ["monitoring"]="monitoring-stack"
    ["harbor"]="harbor"
    ["external-secrets"]="external-secrets"
)

for ns in "${!ns_to_app[@]}"; do
    app="${ns_to_app[$ns]}"
    status=$(argocd app get "$app" -o json 2>/dev/null | jq -r '.status.sync.status // "Unknown"')
    printf "%-20s %-30s %s\n" "$ns" "$app" "$status"
done
```

sections.title: Process substitution — <() and >()
sections.body:
## Process Substitution: Pipes Without the Subshell Problem

Bash pipelines are elegant but have a fundamental limitation that surprises many experienced shell users: **every component of a pipeline runs in a subshell**. Variables set inside a pipeline stage are invisible to the parent shell after the pipeline completes. This is not a bug — it is how process isolation works — but it causes real problems when you try to accumulate state across a loop that reads from a pipe.

Process substitution (`<(cmd)` and `>(cmd)`) is the solution. Instead of piping output from one command to another, process substitution wraps a command in a file-like object (actually a named pipe, `/dev/fd/N`) that another command can read from or write to as if it were a file. The critical difference: the command on the **outside** of the `<(...)` runs in the current shell, not a subshell. This means variables set in a `while read` loop that reads from `< <(cmd)` persist after the loop ends.

This distinction — `cmd | while read` (subshell, variables lost) versus `while read; done < <(cmd)` (current shell, variables kept) — is one of the most practically important bash subtleties. It appears in every serious bash script that accumulates a count, builds an array, or sets a flag while processing lines from a command.

The `<(cmd)` form also enables elegant comparisons between two live commands — `diff <(kubectl get pods -n staging) <(kubectl get pods -n prod)` — without creating temporary files. Combined with `readarray -t arr < <(cmd)` for safely populating arrays from command output, process substitution is a daily tool for anyone writing production-quality bash.

**Why:** sometimes you need to feed command output to something that expects a file, or compare two commands' output without temp files. Process substitution gives you a named pipe on the fly.

```bash
# <(cmd) — treat cmd's output as a file

# Compare two kubectl outputs side by side
diff <(kubectl get pods -n staging) <(kubectl get pods -n prod)

# readarray from a command (you saw this above)
readarray -t pods < <(kubectl get pods -A --no-headers | awk '{print $2}')

# while read loop without a subshell (critical difference!)
# BAD: runs in subshell, variable changes are lost after loop
kubectl get pods | while read -r line; do
    count=$((count + 1))  # count is lost after the pipe
done

# GOOD: process substitution keeps variables in current shell
count=0
while IFS= read -r line; do
    count=$((count + 1))
done < <(kubectl get pods -A --no-headers)
echo "Total pods: $count"  # works!

# >(cmd) — feed output of a command into another command as a file
# tee to two different processors at once
kubectl get pods -A -o json | tee >(jq '.items | length' > /tmp/pod-count.txt) | jq -r '.items[] | .metadata.name'

# Join two sorted lists
join <(sort file1.txt) <(sort file2.txt)
```

sections.title: Advanced patterns: nameref, mapfile, indirect expansion
sections.body:
## Advanced Array Patterns: nameref, mapfile, and Indirect Expansion

Once you are comfortable with the basics of indexed and associative arrays, a few advanced patterns significantly expand what you can do with them. These are not everyday tools, but they appear in well-written library code and in scripts that need to work generically across different data structures.

**Nameref** (`declare -n`) solves the problem of passing arrays to functions. Bash does not have true pass-by-reference, and you cannot pass an array to a function by value (the array gets flattened into separate arguments). The traditional workaround — passing the array name as a string and using indirect expansion — is awkward. Nameref creates a genuine reference: a variable that acts as an alias for another variable, including arrays. Declaring `local -n items=$1` inside a function makes `items` behave exactly like the array whose name was passed in.

**Indirect expansion** (`${!var_name}`) lets you dynamically choose which variable to read based on the value of another variable. This is powerful for dynamic dispatch — selecting configuration based on environment, routing to different handlers based on a resource type — but it can make code harder to follow. When you find yourself reaching for indirect expansion frequently, consider whether an associative array would express the same intent more clearly.

**`mapfile`** (also called `readarray`) with callback (`-C` and `-c` flags) enables processing lines as they are read rather than waiting for the full array to be populated. This is rarely needed but useful for very large inputs where you want to show progress or process in chunks.

These patterns appear most often in library code that must work generically — functions that operate on whatever array the caller passes in, or configuration systems that build variable names from environment names dynamically.

```bash
# nameref — reference another variable by name (bash 4.3+)
declare -n ref=myvar
myvar="hello"
echo "$ref"   # hello — ref IS myvar
ref="world"
echo "$myvar" # world

# Useful for passing array names to functions
process_list() {
    local -n items=$1   # nameref to the array passed by name
    for item in "${items[@]}"; do
        echo "Processing: $item"
    done
}

my_pods=("pod-a" "pod-b" "pod-c")
process_list my_pods   # pass array by name, not by value

# mapfile / readarray — read lines into array
mapfile -t namespaces < <(kubectl get namespaces -o jsonpath='{.items[*].metadata.name}' | tr ' ' '\n')

# mapfile with transformation (-C callback every N lines)
mapfile -t -C 'echo "Read line:"' -c 1 lines < /etc/hosts

# Indirect expansion — variable whose value is another variable's name
ENV=prod
prod_context="eks-prod-mach-x7kq"
var_name="${ENV}_context"
echo "${!var_name}"   # eks-prod-mach-x7kq

# Practical: select kubeconfig based on ENV variable
for ENV in prod staging dev; do
    context_var="${ENV}_context"
    declare "${ENV}_context"="eks-${ENV}"
done
echo "${!prod_context}"  # eks-prod... wait, this gets tricky fast
# Prefer associative arrays for this case
```

sections.title: Cheat sheet
sections.body:
## Quick Reference: Arrays and Process Substitution

This cheat sheet condenses the most frequently used array and process substitution syntax into a single scannable reference. Keep it in mind as you write scripts — the correct syntax for the less common operations (slicing, key existence checks, process substitution variants) is easy to forget and quick to look up here.

The "common mistakes" section at the bottom is particularly important: the two patterns listed there (`arr=($(...))` and `cmd | while read`) are the most common sources of hard-to-debug array and loop bugs in bash scripts. If a script is behaving unexpectedly with arrays or with variables inside loops, check for these patterns first.

```bash
# ── Indexed arrays ──────────────────────────────
arr=(a b c)              # declare
arr+=(d)                 # append
${arr[0]}                # first element
${arr[-1]}               # last element
${arr[@]}                # all elements (use in loops)
${#arr[@]}               # length
${arr[@]:1:2}            # slice: 2 elements starting at index 1
readarray -t arr < <(cmd) # safe: populate from command
for x in "${arr[@]}"; do  # safe iteration

# ── Associative arrays ───────────────────────────
declare -A map
map[key]=value
${map[key]}              # access
${!map[@]}               # all keys
${map[@]}                # all values
[[ -v map[key] ]]        # key exists?

# ── Process substitution ─────────────────────────
diff <(cmd1) <(cmd2)     # compare two commands
while read -r x; do      # loop without subshell
  ...
done < <(cmd)
readarray -t arr < <(cmd) # populate array from cmd

# ── Common mistakes ──────────────────────────────
# WRONG: arr=($(...))    -- breaks on spaces/globs
# RIGHT: readarray -t arr < <(...)

# WRONG: cmd | while read  -- changes lost (subshell)
# RIGHT: while read; done < <(cmd)

# WRONG: for x in ${arr[@]}  -- breaks on spaces
# RIGHT: for x in "${arr[@]}"
```

sections.title: Quiz
sections.body:
## Knowledge Check: Arrays and Process Substitution

This quiz tests understanding of the array and process substitution concepts from the lesson. The questions focus on the practical gotchas that cause real bugs in production scripts: the difference between `[@]` and `[*]`, the subshell problem with pipes, the right tool for key-value lookups, and what `readarray -t` gives you that `arr=($(cmd))` doesn't.

Work through the questions before looking at the answers. The goal is not to have memorized the syntax, but to understand the **why** behind each behavior — because understanding why means you can reason through new situations rather than just pattern-matching to remembered rules.

Answer these before checking — think it through first.

**Q1.** What's the difference between `${arr[@]}` and `${arr[*]}`?

**Q2.** Why does `cmd | while read -r line; do count=$((count+1)); done; echo $count` print 0?

**Q3.** You have a script that receives an environment name (`prod`, `staging`) and needs to look up its kubecontext. What's the cleanest bash approach?

**Q4.** What does `readarray -t` do that plain `arr=($(cmd))` doesn't?

---

**Answers:**

**A1.** With double quotes: `"${arr[@]}"` expands each element as a separate word (safe). `"${arr[*]}"` joins all elements with the first char of IFS (usually a space) into one word.

**A2.** The `while` loop runs in a subshell (due to the pipe). Variables modified in a subshell don't persist to the parent. Fix: `while read -r line; do ...; done < <(cmd)`.

**A3.** Associative array: `declare -A ctx=([prod]=eks-prod [staging]=eks-staging)` then `${ctx[$ENV]}`.

**A4.** `readarray -t` reads each line as a separate array element and strips the trailing newline (`-t`). `arr=($(cmd))` does word-splitting on spaces AND glob-expands, breaking on filenames with spaces or special chars.

---

**Exercise:** Try this in the terminal:

```bash
# Build a namespace health map
declare -A health

readarray -t namespaces < <(kubectl get namespaces --no-headers | awk '{print $1}')

for ns in "${namespaces[@]}"; do
    bad=$(kubectl get pods -n "$ns" --no-headers 2>/dev/null \
        | grep -cv Running || true)
    health[$ns]=$bad
done

echo "Namespace health report:"
for ns in "${!health[@]}"; do
    count=${health[$ns]}
    if [[ $count -gt 0 ]]; then
        echo "  [$count issues] $ns"
    else
        echo "  [OK] $ns"
    fi
done | sort
```
